what: Dycom Industries builds telecommunications networks. Its crews bury and string fibre-optic cable, install the equipment at either end, connect homes and businesses, and increasingly build the electrical and fibre infrastructure that data centres need.
customers: Telephone and cable companies, fibre-to-the-home builders, wireless carriers and, more recently, data centre developers and electric utilities. Work comes through master service agreements and project contracts.
money: Engineering, placing and splicing fibre, installing equipment and connecting customer premises.
Utility line work, locating services and installation for power and gas clients.
moat: Having tens of thousands of trained crews under master service agreements is the asset. Carriers awarding a multi-year fibre programme need a contractor who can mobilise in many states at once, and only a handful can. Long-term agreements make Dycom the default choice for follow-on work in each market.
risks: Revenue depends heavily on a few very large customers' capital budgets. If a major carrier slows its fibre programme, the effect is immediate.
Debt is about $3.0B against $709.2M of cash, raised partly to fund acquisitions.
Eleven analysts average a $513.18 target against a $221.36 price. A gap of over 130% is implausibly wide and should be treated with caution rather than as a forecast.
This is fixed-price contracting at scale: underestimating labour or ground conditions on a programme turns margin into loss.
Government subsidy programmes for rural broadband have been a growth driver, and their funding is finite and politically contingent.
opportunities: Revenue has grown every year shown, from $3.1B in 2022 to $5.5B in 2026, with trailing revenue of about $6.9B.
Data centres need fibre and power connections, which has opened a second large market beyond carrier networks.
The shares trade at about 20 times earnings and 14 times free cash flow, modest for this growth rate.
Free cash flow of $468.7M exceeds net income of $329.6M, a sign of real cash generation rather than accounting profit.
watch: Backlog and the mix within it. The order book shows whether the data centre work is genuinely replacing any slowdown in carrier fibre spending, which is the central question for the next two years.
